title: Memory Leak Detection Per Process
exclusions: Identifies long-lived Linux process candidates whose resident set size grows repeatedly; it does not prove that memory is unreachable, distinguish private from shared pages, measure proportional set size, profile application allocations, diagnose kernel leaks, or predict when an out-of-memory kill will occur. It cannot reliably join a process across a restart because the supplied Linux `ps.sh` output has no process-start field, and it does not observe processes that begin and end between polls. The rule is host-PID-command scoped, has no built-in exception lookup, and makes no compliance claim.
evidence: When deployed, retain the `linux_process_rss_sustained_growth_6h` saved-search export, its schedule and alert history, the returned host/PID/command and six-bucket measurements, and the underlying `sourcetype=ps` snapshots for the alert window. These artifacts demonstrate that indexed RSS values met the configured candidate rule; they do not prove a leak, collection completeness, root cause, or remediation.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated test index with the `Splunk_TA_nix` search-time knowledge, index six complete `sourcetype=ps` table snapshots for `host=rss-leak-positive`, one in each of six consecutive closed hourly buckets. Each table must contain `PID=4242`, `COMMAND=leak-worker`, `USER=svc_test`, and current `RSS` values of 512000, 552960, 593920, 634880, 624640, and 665600 KiB in chronological order. Run a copy of the SPL with fixed bounds for those buckets. Expect exactly one row: `observed_buckets=6`, `comparable_steps=5`, `increase_steps=4`, `growth_kib=153600`, `growth_mib=150`, and `growth_pct=30`.
controlTest.negativeScenario: In a separate six-bucket window, index equivalent complete tables for `host=rss-leak-negative`, `PID=5252`, `COMMAND=cache-worker`, and `USER=svc_test`, with `RSS` values 512000, 522240, 532480, 542720, 552960, and 563200 KiB. Expect zero final rows even though all five transitions increase, because the net change is only 51200 KiB (50 MiB) and 10 percent, below both configured growth thresholds. Inspect the pipeline before the final `where` to confirm six observations and five increases, proving threshold rejection rather than extraction failure.

dataSources: `index=os sourcetype=ps` multi-line process snapshots from the `ps.sh` scripted event input supplied by the Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833). `multikv` expands the table. Required current fields are `PID`, `RSS`, `COMMAND`, and `USER`; the documented legacy RSS alias `RSZ_KB` is also accepted. `_time` and `host` are Splunk metadata. Linux `ps` reports RSS in KiB. The `os` index name and five-minute collection interval are explicit deployment choices.
app: Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833), deployed to Linux collection forwarders and to the Splunk tiers that need its parsing and search-time knowledge.
spl:
index=os sourcetype=ps host=* earliest=-7h@h latest=-1h@h
| multikv
| eval process_id=tostring(PID), process_name=trim(COMMAND), process_user=trim(USER), rss_kib=tonumber(trim(tostring(coalesce(RSS,RSZ_KB))))
| where match(process_id,"^[0-9]+$") AND isnotnull(process_name) AND len(process_name)>0 AND isnotnull(rss_kib) AND rss_kib>0
| bin _time span=1h
| stats latest(rss_kib) as rss_kib latest(process_user) as process_user by _time host process_id process_name
| sort 0 host process_id process_name _time
| streamstats current=f window=1 last(rss_kib) as prior_rss_kib by host process_id process_name
| eval comparable_step=if(isnotnull(prior_rss_kib),1,0), increase_step=if(isnotnull(prior_rss_kib) AND rss_kib>prior_rss_kib,1,0)
| stats earliest(rss_kib) as initial_rss_kib latest(rss_kib) as current_rss_kib count as observed_buckets sum(comparable_step) as comparable_steps sum(increase_step) as increase_steps earliest(_time) as first_bucket latest(_time) as last_bucket latest(process_user) as process_user by host process_id process_name
| eval growth_kib=current_rss_kib-initial_rss_kib, growth_mib=round(growth_kib/1024,1), growth_pct=round(100*growth_kib/initial_rss_kib,1), initial_rss_mib=round(initial_rss_kib/1024,1), current_rss_mib=round(current_rss_kib/1024,1), required_buckets=6, required_comparable_steps=5, required_increase_steps=4, growth_threshold_mib=100, growth_threshold_pct=20
| where observed_buckets=required_buckets AND comparable_steps=required_comparable_steps AND increase_steps>=required_increase_steps AND growth_kib>=growth_threshold_mib*1024 AND growth_pct>=growth_threshold_pct
| convert ctime(first_bucket) ctime(last_bucket)
| table first_bucket last_bucket host process_id process_name process_user initial_rss_mib current_rss_mib growth_kib growth_mib growth_pct observed_buckets comparable_steps increase_steps required_increase_steps growth_threshold_mib growth_threshold_pct
| sort 0 -growth_mib host process_id
description: Detects sustained RSS growth and returns one row per Linux host, process identifier, and command when that identity is present in all six closed hourly buckets, rises in at least four of five bucket-to-bucket comparisons, and increases by both at least 100 MiB and at least 20 percent. The result is an investigation candidate, not proof of a memory leak.
value: Early identification of steadily expanding processes gives service owners time to collect allocator or runtime diagnostics and plan a controlled restart or code fix before memory pressure causes latency, reclaim activity, container eviction, or an out-of-memory termination. Absolute and relative gates reduce pages for harmless movement in both tiny and already-large processes.
implementation: Enable the add-on's supplied `ps.sh` scripted event input on Linux forwarders, route it to the deliberately selected `os` event index, and verify that `multikv` yields numeric `PID` plus current `RSS`, `COMMAND`, and `USER` fields. Collect every five minutes, run the saved search hourly over six closed buckets with a one-hour arrival delay, and alert when result count is greater than zero. Treat 100 MiB, 20 percent, and four increasing transitions as measured starting policy, not Linux or Splunk defaults.
visualization: Use a latest-candidates table showing host, PID, command, user, initial/current RSS MiB, absolute and percentage growth, and increasing-step count. Add a drilldown line chart of hourly RSS MiB for the selected host-PID-command and a separate collection-health panel showing last `sourcetype=ps` event time per host. Do not label the chart as confirmed leaked bytes.
dataModelAcceleration: The add-on classifies `sourcetype=ps` as Performance data, but CIM Performance 6.4 has no per-process PID, command, or RSS-growth dataset. No equivalent accelerated `tstats` search is claimed; the raw table and add-on-specific process fields are required.

knownFalsePositives:
1. **Java HotSpot heap expansion or cache warm-up** — A JVM can retain a larger committed heap after startup or a traffic step without leaking unreachable objects. Compare the alert window with full-GC behavior, heap-after-GC, class-loader counts, and an application heap dump; suppress only a measured warm-up period for the exact service and host.

2. **PostgreSQL worker and shared-memory behavior** — RSS can include resident shared mappings, and backend PIDs turn over. Check the process start time, PostgreSQL role, shared-buffer settings, workload, and proportional/private memory in `/proc/<pid>/smaps_rollup` before attributing growth to one backend.

3. **glibc allocator retention after a bounded batch** — An application can free objects while its allocator keeps arenas mapped for reuse. Distinguish this from live-object growth with an application-appropriate heap profiler and compare `RssAnon`, PSS, and post-idle behavior rather than relying on RSS alone.

4. **Service restart followed by Linux PID reuse** — The add-on's current Linux `ps.sh` fields do not include process start time. A new process can inherit the same PID and command during the six-hour window. Compare `/proc/<pid>/stat` start time, systemd journal entries, and deployment records; rerun the observation window after the restart.

5. **Fork, copy-on-write, and changing shared mappings** — Prefork servers and mapped files can change per-process RSS as pages become resident even when private allocations are stable. Use `/proc/<pid>/smaps_rollup`, PSS, `RssAnon`, worker-generation metadata, and the parent/child topology to distinguish mapping residency from a leak.

6. **Approved load or soak test** — A named test may intentionally drive caches and heap growth. If paging is inappropriate, use an owner-approved `linux_process_memory_exceptions.csv` lookup keyed by exact `host` and `process_name`, with `start_epoch`, `end_epoch`, `reason`, `ticket`, and `approver`. Apply the time-bound exception only after the base result is preserved; reject wildcards and non-expiring entries.
mitreAttack: N/A (operational Linux process-memory monitoring; no adversary behavior asserted)
reviewer: documentation editorial review against Splunk and Linux primary sources; no runtime validation or SME sign-off
detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and interpretation boundary

Install a currently supported release of the Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833) on each Linux collection forwarder, and deploy its parsing and search-time knowledge to the tiers required by the local Splunk topology. Confirm the current Splunkbase compatibility table before installation or upgrade. The listing warns that version 6.0 changed default indexes and configuration files, so test an upgrade outside production. Follow Splunk's documented script execution and operating-system privilege requirements, and grant the monitoring role read access only to the selected operating-system index plus the capability to schedule this search.

This use case is deliberately a candidate detector. Linux `ps` defines RSS as non-swapped physical memory used by a task, in KiB. RSS includes resident mappings and does not say whether application objects remain reachable; kernel documentation also separates anonymous, file-backed, and shared resident memory. Repeated RSS growth can justify investigation, but cannot by itself prove a user-space leak. The title is retained as the catalogue identity, while alert text and dashboards must say “sustained RSS growth candidate.”

## 1. Enable and verify process collection

Use the `ps.sh` scripted event input shipped with the add-on. On a Universal Forwarder, copy only its exact stanza from `Splunk_TA_nix/default/inputs.conf` into `Splunk_TA_nix/local/inputs.conf`, set `disabled = 0`, set `interval = 300`, and set `index = os`. Do not copy the complete default file; Splunk documents that local settings persist across upgrades. `index=os` and the five-minute interval are this deployment design, not immutable product defaults. If governance selects another event index, change the input and the SPL together. A complete process table every five minutes can be high volume on dense hosts, so estimate ingest and search load before fleet rollout.

After deployment, inspect the effective input with `splunk btool inputs list --debug` and confirm events with `index=os sourcetype=ps earliest=-15m`. The raw event must preserve the table header and aligned rows. Run `index=os sourcetype=ps earliest=-15m | multikv | table _time host PID RSS RSZ_KB COMMAND USER`. Splunk documents that `multikv` creates one event per table row and derives names from the header. Current add-on output for Linux uses `RSS`; the add-on's 8.7.0 mapping table identifies legacy `RSZ_KB` as its equivalent and states that backward-compatible older fields are retained. The SPL coalesces both but treats `RSS` as canonical. Reject a deployment where neither field is numeric.

On a staging host, compare the same collection instant with `ps -eo user:32,pid,rss,stat,lstart,comm,args --sort=pid`. Allow for script execution, forwarding, and indexing delay. Verify several PIDs and RSS values, not just the largest process. The `ps` manual reports RSS in KiB, so the search divides by 1024 to display MiB. Check command truncation: Splunk documents a 100-character `COMMAND` limit in the supplied script unless it is deliberately changed. Record any local script modification because it affects process grouping and upgrade support.

## 2. Save and understand the search

Save the catalogue SPL as `linux_process_rss_sustained_growth_6h` and schedule it hourly shortly after the hour. The explicit `earliest=-7h@h latest=-1h@h` bounds select six closed hourly buckets and leave one hour for late data. This delay is conservative; change it only after measuring end-to-end arrival latency. Trigger when result count is greater than zero and include every returned field in the alert payload.

`multikv` expands each snapshot. The first `eval` converts `PID` to the process identity, keeps `COMMAND` and `USER`, coalesces current `RSS` with documented legacy `RSZ_KB`, and converts RSS to a number. The `where` removes headers, malformed rows, zero RSS, and rows without enough identity. `bin` and the first `stats` retain the chronologically latest sample for each host-PID-command in each hour, preventing a five-minute polling cadence from overweighting an hour. `sort 0` orders each identity from oldest to newest; `streamstats current=f window=1` then exposes the prior hourly RSS. The next aggregation requires six observed buckets and five comparable transitions.

The final policy requires at least four increasing transitions, at least 102400 KiB (100 MiB) net growth, and at least 20 percent growth from the first to last bucket. All three conditions must hold. These values are catalogue starting points, not limits published by Linux, procps, or Splunk. Four-of-five allows one garbage-collection or reclaim dip while still demanding repeated growth. The absolute gate prevents a tiny process from paging on a large percentage; the relative gate prevents an already-large process from paging on inconsequential movement. Baseline by service class for at least one representative business cycle, then document every threshold change with owner and date.

Identity is `host + PID + COMMAND`. Current Linux add-on output removed `ELAPSED`, so there is no supported start-time field to prevent PID reuse. Grouping by command reduces but does not eliminate restart collisions. Do not group only by command: multiple workers would be merged into a fabricated process. Do not group only by PID across hosts. If reliable process-start identity is mandatory, design and validate a separate approved collector rather than claiming that this rule provides it.

The add-on's source-type table maps `ps` to CIM Performance, but CIM Performance 6.4 models host-level memory fields and does not define per-process PID, command, or RSS history. No `cimSpl` is supplied because an accelerated `tstats` query would change the signal. Do not claim data-model acceleration for this search path.

## 3. Validate extraction and detection logic

Build test events as complete aligned `ps` tables with a header, because table extraction is part of the control. Place the six positive values from `controlTest` in consecutive closed hourly buckets. Add at least one unrelated healthy process to every snapshot so the fixture resembles a table rather than pre-populated scalar fields. Run a copy of the SPL against the isolated index with fixed absolute earliest/latest bounds. Expect one result with six buckets, five comparable steps, four increasing steps, 150 MiB growth, and 30 percent growth. Verify the initial and current MiB values are 500 and 650.

Run the negative values in a separate window. Before the final `where`, expect six buckets, five comparable and increasing transitions, 50 MiB growth, and 10 percent growth; after the filter, expect zero rows. Add three failure controls: omit one hourly snapshot and expect rejection by `observed_buckets`; change `RSS` to `?` and expect that row to be discarded by numeric conversion; reuse PID 4242 with a different `COMMAND` and confirm it forms a separate identity rather than bridging the series.

For staging validation, compare at least six indexed buckets with on-host `ps`. Confirm the selected hourly sample is the latest `_time` in each bucket and that late arrivals fit inside the one-hour delay. Track collection separately with `index=os sourcetype=ps | stats latest(_time) as last_seen count by host`; a quiet candidate search is not evidence that collection is healthy. This editorial review verified documentation and search logic only. It did not run the fixture in Splunk, execute the collector on Linux, or validate a production platform/add-on combination, which is why the sidecar remains `status=draft`.

## 4. Alert, investigate, and visualize

Route the alert to the owning service team, deduplicate on host, PID, and command for one search interval, and retain continued measurements rather than applying a day-long throttle. The first response is confirmation, not an automatic restart. On the host, run `ps -p <pid> -o pid,ppid,user,rss,vsz,stat,lstart,comm,args` and verify that the start time predates the six-hour window. Inspect `/proc/<pid>/status` for `VmRSS`, `RssAnon`, `RssFile`, and `RssShmem`; where permitted, use `/proc/<pid>/smaps_rollup` for RSS and PSS. Compare service logs, deployment history, request volume, cache state, container or cgroup limits, swap/reclaim pressure, and OOM messages.

Escalate to the application owner with diagnostics appropriate to the runtime: for example, heap-after-GC and a heap dump for Java, allocator or object profiles for native code, or runtime-specific allocation telemetry. A controlled restart can mitigate pressure but erases evidence and does not repair a leak. Never make this alert kill a PID or restart a service automatically. Confirm service dependencies, capture diagnostics, and use the approved change process.

Display a candidates table and an identity-specific hourly line chart. The line chart should plot RSS MiB and annotate the 100 MiB and 20 percent policy, but must not call the y-axis “leaked memory.” Add a separate panel for source freshness and extraction failures such as missing `RSS`; otherwise a broken collector can look like a healthy fleet. Restrict access to `COMMAND` and especially raw `ARGS`, because applications can expose secrets in command lines.

## 5. Preserve evidence, troubleshoot, and suppress safely

Retain the saved-search definition, scheduler history, alert result, six source snapshots, and incident record according to the operations retention policy. Record whether on-host PID/start-time verification succeeded, which memory diagnostic was used, the owner's conclusion, and any remediation. These artifacts support operational review; they do not establish a regulatory control or prove all allocations were observed.

No `ps` data usually indicates that the input remains disabled, the add-on is absent from the forwarder, execution permissions or the vendor-documented runtime privilege are missing, routing sends events to another index, or the search role cannot read the index. Raw tables without fields usually mean the header was altered, search-time knowledge is absent, the source type changed, or an ingest transformation damaged alignment. Use `btool`, forwarder `splunkd.log`, and the add-on's documented script debug procedure to isolate collection from parsing failures. If only `RSZ_KB` appears, legacy compatibility is working; if both RSS names are absent, repair extraction rather than inventing an undocumented field.

The base SPL deliberately contains no lookup, so its behavior is reviewable. For a sanctioned load test or known warm-up, preserve the base match and then apply an optional `linux_process_memory_exceptions.csv` lookup keyed by exact host and command, active only between approved start and end epochs. Require reason, ticket, approver, and owner; reject wildcards, PID-only entries, and permanent expiry. Review suppressed candidates on the same cadence as alerts. Do not suppress a whole host merely because one service has expected growth, and do not carry an exception across a software release without re-baselining.
grandmaExplanation: We watch each long-running program to see whether the memory it keeps in use rises again and again over several hours. That gives the team an early clue to investigate before the server runs short of room, while recognizing that growth alone does not prove a bug.
